reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / AAO Basic and Clinical Science Course
clinicalPearls: Phacodonesis is a tremulous, wobbling movement of the crystalline lens seen on ocular saccades, signifying loss of zonular integrity and impending or partial lens subluxation
It is a clinical sign rather than a diagnosis, and its presence should trigger a search for the underlying cause of zonular weakness
In adults the commonest cause is pseudoexfoliation syndrome, in which fibrillar deposits progressively degrade the zonular attachments
Blunt or penetrating ocular trauma is a frequent cause and may produce localised zonular dialysis with sectoral phacodonesis
Heritable connective-tissue disorders are key associations, notably Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1), homocystinuria and Weill-Marchesani syndrome, and their systemic features must be sought
It is best elicited at the slit lamp by asking the patient to make quick eye movements and observing oscillation of the lens, often accompanied by iridodonesis (tremulous iris)
Phacodonesis markedly increases the risk of intra-operative complications such as zonular dialysis, capsular instability and dropped lens fragments, so it must be documented before cataract surgery
Progression to frank lens subluxation or complete dislocation into the anterior chamber or vitreous can precipitate pupillary-block or lens-induced glaucoma
reference.pathophysiology: The crystalline lens is suspended by the ciliary zonule, a system of fibrillin-rich microfibrils running from the ciliary body to the lens capsule that holds the lens centred and taut. Phacodonesis results when these fibres are reduced in number, stretched or disrupted, so the lens is inadequately anchored and oscillates with inertial movement of the eye. In pseudoexfoliation, abnormal fibrillar material and enzymatic degradation weaken the zonular insertions. In Marfan syndrome, mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene yield structurally deficient microfibrils; in homocystinuria, accumulated homocysteine disrupts zonular cross-linking; and trauma mechanically avulses zonular fibres. The common endpoint is a loss of stable zonular support that permits abnormal lens mobility and predisposes to subluxation.
additionalDifferentials: Weill-Marchesani syndrome and other microspherophakia-associated laxity
High axial myopia or buphthalmos with stretched zonules
Zonular weakness after prior vitreoretinal surgery
additionalInvestigations: Dilated slit-lamp examination to grade lens movement, zonular gaps and any subluxation
Gonioscopy and intraocular pressure measurement to assess angle status and glaucoma risk
Ultrasound biomicroscopy to image the zonule, ciliary body and degree of lens decentration
Search for pseudoexfoliation material on the pupillary margin and anterior capsule
Plasma and urine homocysteine and amino-acid studies where homocystinuria is suspected
Systemic evaluation and echocardiography for Marfan syndrome and related connective-tissue disease
Genetic testing (for example FBN1) guided by the clinical phenotype
redFlags: Acute lens-induced or pupillary-block angle closure with pain and pressure rise
Complete lens dislocation into the anterior chamber threatening corneal decompensation
Features of Marfan syndrome warranting cardiovascular assessment for aortic root dilatation
Homocystinuria with its risk of thromboembolism
Sudden change from lens tremulousness to frank dislocation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and on early recognition; with careful surgical planning using capsular support devices, good visual outcomes are achievable, though the presence of phacodonesis raises the risk of intra-operative and postoperative complications. Untreated progression to dislocation and secondary glaucoma can threaten sight and, in syndromic causes, systemic morbidity may dominate.
pitfalls: Overlooking subtle phacodonesis and encountering unexpected zonular dialysis during cataract surgery
Failing to identify pseudoexfoliation as the underlying cause in an older patient
Missing a systemic diagnosis such as Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria with life-threatening implications
Not measuring intraocular pressure and assessing the angle in a mobile lens
Assuming a stable lens when only iridodonesis is noted without testing lens movement
